quotes.quote: Refusal is only one third of willpower. When a lapse repeats, ask which power went quiet before you call yourself weak.
quotes.why: Strongest compact reframing of the chapter's core move.

quotes.quote: A goal must be present to have power.
quotes.why: Memorable mechanism line that makes the advice portable.

quotes.quote:
a) Being important is not the same as being vivid; a value can matter and still lose to a cue that feels louder right now.
   b) The long-term goal needs attention at the choice point to compete.
quotes.why: Worst quiz defect: both choices are supported by the prose.

quotes.quote: If-then 1: [If your hand moves before your reason catches up] If your hand moves before your reason catches up,
quotes.why: The duplicated bracketed cue creates a visible scaffold smell.

a is the only balanced option; b and c contain giveaway absolutist language.

complaints.problem: Choices a and b are both directly supported: a states the vividness/value mechanism and b states the choice-point attention mechanism, so a single key is underdetermined.
Several distractors are extreme or obviously anti-method, and correct choices often echo chapter wording or are uniquely nuanced, making them easier to guess without reading closely.
The if-then lines repeat the bracketed cue immediately in the sentence, which reads like unresolved template scaffolding.
The why-it-matters lines repeatedly invoke Miller/Cohen without adding much new causal detail, so the later examples feel less distinct than the earlier ones.

parsedReview.oneParagraphVerdict: This is a strong, beginner-friendly chapter with a memorable central move, concrete images, and a practical exercise that a reader could actually try. The blocker is the quiz: Q6 has two defensible answers, and several other questions are weakened by obvious distractors and answer-shape tells. Repairing that quiz ambiguity and polishing the scaffold smell in the implementation plan would likely bring it over a professional ship bar.
